h1: Compact laminate vs laminate: what is the difference?
lead: The surface is the same hard laminate, but laminate is a thin layer glued to a wood-based board, while compact laminate is laminate all the way through. The difference shows when water reaches an edge.
body:
Compact laminate or laminate is a choice that comes up again and again in specifications for built-in furniture in schools and institutions. The surface looks the same and feels the same, so the difference lies underneath. Laminate is a thin layer glued onto a core board of chipboard or MDF. Compact laminate is the same material pressed into a board that is laminate all the way through. That decides where each of them can be used.

## How the boards are built

Laminate, or HPL for high-pressure laminate, is made from layers of paper soaked in resin and pressed together under high pressure and heat. The top layer carries the colour or decor. As the surface of a piece of furniture, the laminate is thin and glued to a core board, and the edges are closed with edge banding.

Melamine looks similar but is something else. Here a single layer of resin-impregnated paper is pressed directly onto the chipboard. It is cheaper than laminate and takes less wear and fewer knocks, and it is the white surface most people know from cabinets and shelves.

Compact laminate is laminate in full thickness. There are so many layers of paper and resin that the board becomes solid and can carry itself. The core is usually black and shows as a stripe on the edge, and boards with a coloured core are available.

## What happens when water reaches the edge

The surface is tight on both boards. It is the edge that makes the difference. On laminate on a core board, the edge is edge banding glued to chipboard or MDF, and every hole for a hinge or a pipe goes through the laminate and into the wood. If water stands at an edge or in a hole, the core board soaks it up. Chipboard and MDF swell when they get wet, and they do not shrink back when they dry again. The edge banding comes loose, and the furniture has to be replaced.

Moisture-resistant chipboard and MDF last longer in damp rooms, but they are still wood, and if they stand in water, they are damaged.

Compact laminate has no core that can soak up water. An edge or a drilled hole is the same dense material as the surface, so the board can stand in a room where there is water on the floor and where the furniture is washed down every day.

## Where each of them belongs

| Property | Laminate on a core board | Compact laminate |
|---|---|---|
| Build-up | Thin laminate glued to chipboard or MDF | Laminate all the way through |
| Edges | Closed with edge banding | Sanded and left visible with the core |
| Water | Takes water on the surface, not in edges and holes | Takes water everywhere |
| Self-supporting | No, sits in a piece of furniture | Yes, e.g. as a partition on legs |
| Weight | Like the core board | Heavier than a wood-based board |
| Price | Cheapest | More expensive |

Laminate on a core board is a good and cheaper choice for cabinets and fronts in dry rooms, such as classrooms and offices. Compact laminate belongs where water hits the furniture, in toilets and changing rooms. Read about [toilet cubicles](/toiletbaase) and [cabinets in compact laminate](/kompaktlaminat-skabe).

Between the two are rooms that are damp without being wet, such as a staff kitchen. Here the cabinets can be laminate on a core board, while the worktop around the sink is compact laminate. That is often where the money is best spent.

## Thickness and machining

The thickness is chosen by what the board has to carry and how far it spans. Partitions and doors in toilet cubicles are typically made of compact laminate of 12 to 13 mm. A wash counter that has to carry a basin and span freely between the brackets is made from a thicker board, e.g. 20 mm.

Compact laminate is heavy and hard, so it is cut and drilled with carbide tools, and it takes longer to machine than a wood-based board. The edges do not need to be closed. They are sanded and chamfered, so the core becomes part of the look. See what we build in [compact laminate](/kompaktlaminat).

## Maintenance

Both surfaces are cleaned with water and ordinary cleaning agents, and neither needs oiling or painting. A deep scratch cannot be sanded away, as it can on oiled wood. If the furniture is mostly worn by knocks and bumps, oiled plywood can therefore be a better choice, because the surface can be refreshed on site. See [plywood, MDF or chipboard](/krydsfiner-mdf-eller-spaanplade).

faq.q: Is compact laminate the same as HPL?
faq.a: Compact laminate is HPL in full thickness. Ordinary HPL is a thin layer of high-pressure laminate glued to a core board. The surface is the same, but compact laminate has no core board that can be damaged by water.

faq.q: Can laminate be used in wet rooms?
faq.a: The surface takes water, but the core board does not. Where water reaches edges and drilled holes, chipboard and MDF will swell sooner or later, and here compact laminate is the safe choice. Laminate on a moisture-resistant core board can be used where there is only moisture in the air.

faq.q: How thick should compact laminate be?
faq.a: It depends on what the board has to carry. For partitions and toilet cubicles 12 to 13 mm is typical, and for wash counters that carry a basin a thicker board, e.g. 20 mm. If the specification requires a certain thickness, that is what applies.

faq.q: Why is compact laminate more expensive than laminate?
faq.a: The board is laminate all the way through instead of a thin layer on a cheaper core board, and it is heavier and takes longer to machine. The edges do not need closing, and the board does not need replacing because it has taken in water.

faq.q: What is the difference between melamine and laminate?
faq.a: Melamine is a single layer of resin-impregnated paper pressed directly onto the chipboard. Laminate is several layers pressed on their own and glued on afterwards, and it takes more wear and more knocks. Both sit on a core board and share the same weakness when water reaches the edge.

highlights.v: Thin layer glued to chipboard or MDF
Laminate all the way through
One layer pressed directly onto the chipboard
The core board swells at the edge, compact laminate does not
Edge banding or a visible core
Thinner for cubicles, thicker for wash counters

h1: Plywood vs MDF vs chipboard for built-in furniture
lead: The three boards look the same on a drawing, but they behave differently once the furniture is in use. Here is what is inside each board, and when MDF or chipboard is the right choice rather than plywood.
body:
Plywood, MDF or chipboard for built-in furniture? For furniture that takes knocks and has to last for many years, plywood is usually right. MDF is right where the surface has to be painted completely smooth or routed into a shape, and melamine-faced chipboard is right for cabinets in dry rooms, where price counts most. The difference lies in what the boards are made of.

Plywood is thin layers of wood glued together with the grain running crosswise. Each layer holds the next, so the board moves far less than solid wood and is strong for its weight. The edge shows the layers as stripes.

MDF is wood fibres pressed together with glue into a dense board with no grain and no layers. It is the same all the way through, so it can be routed into soft shapes and painted without anything showing through.

Chipboard is wood chips pressed together with glue. It is stiff enough for a cabinet and the cheapest of the three, but the chips are coarse, so the board almost always gets a melamine or laminate face and edge banding.

| Property | Plywood | MDF | Chipboard |
|---|---|---|---|
| Screws in the edge | Hold well | Can split the board | Hold worst |
| The edge | Can be left visible | Painted or covered | Covered with edge banding |
| Surface | Oil, lacquer or laminate | Paint or veneer | Melamine or laminate |
| Moisture | Takes moisture, not standing water | Swells, available in moisture-resistant grade | Swells if water reaches the edge |
| Knocks and wear | Can be lightly sanded and oiled | The paint can be touched up | A chip cannot be sanded out |
| Board price | Highest | In the middle | Lowest |

## When MDF is the right choice

MDF is right when the surface has to be painted and completely even, e.g. fronts in the same colour as the wall, or when a panel has to be routed into a shape with soft edges. Because the board has no grain, the paint looks the same across the whole surface, and a routed edge comes out smooth. Plywood can also be painted, but the grain can be seen, and the edge has to be filled if the layers must not show. How plywood is painted is explained in the guide [do you need to prime plywood?](/skal-krydsfiner-grundes)

The weakness is the edge. A screw straight into the edge of MDF can split the board, so joints in the edge are pre-drilled or made with fittings designed for MDF. Ordinary MDF does not take moisture and swells if water gets in, but there are moisture-resistant grades for damp rooms.

## When chipboard is the right choice

Melamine-faced chipboard is right for cabinets that stand in a dry room behind closed doors, such as a storage cabinet or an office cabinet. The melamine is smooth and easy to wipe, and the board is the cheapest way to build many cabinets.

The weakness is here too in the edges. If water gets in under the edge banding, the chips swell, and it cannot be repaired. A knock that chips off a piece of the melamine cannot be sanded out either, and a screw that has come loose grips less well when it is put back in. That is why chipboard is not right for benches and cloakrooms that take knocks every day.

## Plywood where furniture is used hard

Plywood is right where the furniture takes knocks, and where hinges and hooks have to stay put for many years. The board holds screws, also close to the edge, and the edge can be left visible without edge banding. An oiled surface can be refreshed where it is worn. What that looks like in a school or a daycare centre is shown under [plywood furniture](/krydsfiner-inventar).

The boards can also be combined. Both MDF and chipboard can get a surface of real wood, veneer, but the edge still shows the board and has to be covered. A cabinet that stays closed in a dry room can have plywood doors on a melamine carcass. What that means for a cabinet is shown under [plywood cabinets](/skabe-i-krydsfiner).

## When water hits

None of the three boards belongs where water hits directly, as in toilets and at wash counters. Here compact laminate is right, because the board is laminate all the way through and does not soak up water. The difference between compact laminate and laminate on a board is explained in the guide [compact laminate vs laminate](/kompaktlaminat-eller-laminat).

## Certification and documentation

If the tender requires FSC- or PEFC-certified wood, or if the building is to carry the Nordic Swan Ecolabel, the boards must be documented. It is worth clarifying early, because not every board can be supplied with the certification the tender requires. See [furniture for Nordic Swan Ecolabel buildings](/inventar-til-svanemaerket-byggeri).

faq.q: Which is stronger, plywood or MDF?
faq.a: Plywood. The crosswise layers make the board stiff and strong for its weight, and it holds screws in the edge, where MDF can split. MDF, on the other hand, is easier to get completely smooth under paint.

faq.q: When is MDF the right choice?
faq.a: When the surface has to be painted completely even, or a front has to be routed into a shape. In damp rooms it has to be a moisture-resistant grade, and where water hits directly, it should be compact laminate.

faq.q: Can chipboard be used for school furniture?
faq.a: Yes, for cabinets in dry rooms behind closed doors, with melamine or laminate on the surface. For benches, cloakrooms and anything else that takes knocks every day, plywood is the better choice.

faq.q: What board thickness is used for built-in furniture?
faq.a: For carcasses, shelves and doors 18 mm plywood is standard, and melamine-faced chipboard is typically 16 or 19 mm. Long shelves and benches that carry weight get a thicker board or a reinforcement underneath, so they do not bend over time.

faq.q: Which material should be used in wet rooms?
faq.a: None of the three. Where water hits directly, we use compact laminate, which is laminate all the way through and does not soak up water.

highlights.v: Holds screws and takes knocks, the edge can stay visible
Smooth surface for paint and routed shapes
Cheapest, for cabinets in dry rooms
MDF and chipboard are vulnerable at the edge
None of the three, use compact laminate
Clarify FSC, PEFC and Nordic Swan early

h1: What to send when you ask for a price on built-in joinery
lead: A price on built-in joinery is never more precise than the material it is calculated from. Here is what we use each part for, and what happens if it is missing.
body:
When you ask for a price on built-in joinery, the material you send decides how much of the price is calculated and how much is assumed. Whatever is missing, we have to assume, and each assumption appears as a reservation in our offer. The fewer reservations, the easier the offer is to compare with the others you receive.

| What you send | What we use it for | If it is missing |
|---|---|---|
| Drawings with plans, elevations and sections | Dimensions and quantities | We can give an estimate, but not a price per item |
| The full joinery specification | Materials and finishes, product by product | We assume oiled plywood and state it in the offer |
| The bill of quantities | Price per item, as the list stands | We count from the drawings and state the quantities in the offer |
| Requirements for Nordic Swan Ecolabel, FSC or PEFC | Choice of boards and documentation | The boards may be bought before the requirement is known |
| Schedule with installation date | Planning of production and stages | Production cannot be planned yet |
| Site access conditions | Delivery and installation | Installation can take longer than calculated |

## The drawings show what is to be built

The plan shows where the furniture stands and how long it is. The elevations show the height and the division, and they decide how many doors and drawers have to be priced. If the drawings carry item numbers that match the bill of quantities, every price in the offer can be traced back to a drawing. Once the order is placed, we model the furniture in 3D from your drawings, see [shop drawings and 3D model](/vaerkstedstegninger-og-3d-model).

## The whole specification, including the general sections

The joinery specification says what the furniture is to be made of. Requirements for finishes and fittings are often in the general sections and not under the individual item, so send the whole specification and not just the pages about the furniture. Also send the general building specification, because it holds the requirements for documentation and the site that apply to all trades.

Without a specification we assume our starting point, oiled plywood, and state it in the offer, so it can be corrected. If the specification says lacquer, lacquer is what we price. You can read about choosing between the boards in [plywood, MDF or chipboard](/krydsfiner-mdf-eller-spaanplade).

If the building is to carry the Nordic Swan Ecolabel, or the tender requires FSC- or PEFC-certified wood, say so in the enquiry. Certified wood has to be bought as certified, and the documentation is collected while purchasing, so the requirement must be known before the boards are ordered. Not every board is available with certification, and the offer states which ones can be supplied with it. If the building is to be DGNB-certified, the same documentation can be used. See [furniture for Nordic Swan Ecolabel buildings](/inventar-til-svanemaerket-byggeri).

## The bill of quantities decides how the price is set out

If there is a bill of quantities, we price each item as the list stands. If we find a difference between drawing and list, we do not correct the list but state the difference as a reservation. That way your offer can be compared item by item with the other bids on the same list.

If there is no list, we count from the drawings ourselves and state the quantities in the offer, so you can see what the price covers. What we have not priced is also stated in the offer. If the tender has a deadline for questions, that is where uncertainties should be clarified, so the answer reaches everyone bidding. Whatever is not clarified, we state as a reservation.

## The schedule and the conditions on site

Include the installation date, even if it may move. We plan production around it from the start, and if the furniture is to be delivered in stages, we plan production by the stages.

We deliver and install the furniture, so the access conditions affect the price. It makes a difference whether there is a lift, and how close a lorry can get. Also say if there are rooms that will be in use while we install.

## Before the tender, the price can be calculated as an estimate

If the project is at the design stage, we can give an estimate from the material that exists and point out where a choice moves the price. The biggest jump comes from the material: a cabinet in compact laminate costs almost twice as much as the same cabinet in pine plywood. It is easiest to change while the specification can still be altered.

We most often bid for the main contractor, see [built-in joinery as a subcontract](/inventar-til-hovedentreprenoerer). When the furniture is tendered as its own trade package, you as the building owner can also ask us for a price directly. Projects outside Denmark: send us the drawings and we will tell you what we can deliver. Send what you have to tilbud@neminventar.dk.

faq.q: Can you give a price from drawings alone?
faq.a: Yes. Without a joinery specification we assume oiled plywood and state it in the offer as an assumption, so it can be corrected. The more of the specification you send, the fewer assumptions there are.

faq.q: What do you do if the drawing and the bill of quantities do not match?
faq.a: We price the list as it stands and state the difference as a reservation. That way the offer can be compared with the other bids on the same list.

faq.q: Which file formats can you use?
faq.a: PDF is enough to calculate a price.

faq.q: Can we get an estimate before the project goes to tender?
faq.a: Yes. Send the material that exists, and we will give an estimate and point out where a choice of material moves the price while the specification can still be changed.

faq.q: Can we as building owner ask you for a price directly?
faq.a: Yes, when the furniture is tendered as its own trade package. Most often we bid for the main contractor.

faq.q: Should installation be part of the enquiry?
faq.a: We deliver and install the furniture. Describe the access conditions and whether installation is to happen in stages, because both affect how long installation takes.

highlights.v: Plans, elevations and sections, ideally with item numbers
The whole joinery specification with the general sections
Price per item, as the list stands
Nordic Swan Ecolabel, FSC or PEFC from the start
Installation date and any stages

nav_label: Do you need to prime plywood?
h1: Do you need to prime plywood?
lead: Yes, if the plywood is to be painted. No, if it is to be oiled, because the oil has to get into the wood, and a primer would close it off.
body:
Whether plywood needs priming depends on what goes on top. If it is to be painted, yes. If it is to be oiled, no, and if it is to be lacquered, the first coat of lacquer is the primer itself. What all three treatments have to allow for is that plywood absorbs unevenly.

Plywood is thin layers of wood glued together with the grain running crosswise, and only the outer layer is visible. In pine, the light, soft parts of the growth rings absorb more than the dark, hard ones, so the surface takes paint and colour differently. The edge absorbs most, because every other layer shows end grain, and end grain draws liquid further in than the rest of the wood.

That is why paint on untreated plywood often turns out blotchy, and a coloured oil tends to go darker on the edge than on the face.

## If it is to be painted: sand, prime and paint

Plywood that is to be painted is sanded first, so the surface is clean and even. Then it is primed with a wood primer that seals the surface, so the paint lies evenly. A water-based primer raises the wood fibres, so the surface is lightly sanded before painting. Two coats of paint is normal.

On pine plywood, the knots can bleed through a light paint as yellow stains. Here a stain-blocking primer is used that holds back the resin in the knot. The edge gets an extra coat of primer, and if it has to be smooth under the paint, it is filled first, so the layers cannot be seen.

If the furniture has to be painted and completely smooth, MDF is often a better starting point than plywood. See the guide [plywood, MDF or chipboard](/krydsfiner-mdf-eller-spaanplade).

## If it is to be oiled: no primer

Oil has to penetrate the wood and cure there. A primer would close the surface so the oil cannot get in, so it is skipped. The oil is applied in a thin coat, and whatever the wood does not take is wiped off before it cures, so no oil is left standing on the surface.

The advantage shows when the furniture is worn. A worn corner or a scratch is lightly sanded and oiled where the damage is, without the whole surface having to be treated again. That is why oil is our starting point for [plywood furniture](/krydsfiner-inventar) for schools and institutions.

## Colour: stain or coloured oil

Stain colours the wood but does not protect it, so a stained surface needs oil or lacquer on top. Coloured oil gives colour and protection in the same treatment, and the grain shows through the colour.

The same colour looks different on pine and birch and can vary from board to board, because the wood absorbs differently. That is why the colour should be approved on a sample of the board the furniture will be made from. On a cabinet, the doors can be coloured while the rest stays in clear oil, see [plywood cabinets](/skabe-i-krydsfiner).

## If it is to be lacquered: the first coat is the primer

Lacquer lays a film on top of the wood. The first coat acts as a sealer: it closes the surface and raises the fibres, so it is lightly sanded before the next coats are applied. A lacquered surface is closed and easy to wipe. If a scratch goes through the film, moisture and dirt can get in underneath, and if the repair must not show, the whole surface has to be sanded and lacquered again.

Our starting point is oil, but if the joinery specification says lacquer, lacquer is what we price and deliver.

## No treatment makes plywood waterproof

Oil and lacquer protect against moisture from wet jackets and a cloth, but they do not turn plywood into a wet-room board. There is plywood glued with waterproof glue, but the wood in the layers still soaks up water if it stands on the surface or draws into the edge. Where water hits directly, as in toilets and at wash counters, we use [compact laminate](/kompaktlaminat), which is laminate all the way through and needs no treatment.

faq.q: Do you need to prime plywood before painting?
faq.a: Yes. Untreated plywood absorbs unevenly, so the paint turns out blotchy. Sand, prime with a wood primer, sand lightly and paint twice. Give the edge an extra coat of primer, and use a stain-blocking primer on knotty pine under a light colour.

faq.q: Do you need to prime plywood before oiling?
faq.a: No. The oil has to penetrate the wood, and a primer would close the surface so the oil cannot get in.

faq.q: Why does paint look uneven on plywood?
faq.a: Because the surface absorbs differently, and the edge absorbs most. In pine, the soft parts of the growth rings absorb more than the hard ones. A primer seals the surface so the paint lies evenly.

faq.q: Can oiled plywood be repaired?
faq.a: Yes. A worn or scratched spot is lightly sanded and oiled where the damage is, without the whole surface having to be treated again. That is why we use oil on furniture in schools and institutions.

faq.q: How do you maintain oiled plywood?
faq.a: Day to day with a well wrung cloth and a mild cleaning agent. When a spot is worn, it is lightly sanded and oiled with the same oil, and that can be done on site.

faq.q: Can plywood be used in wet rooms?
faq.a: Not where water hits directly. Oil and lacquer do not make plywood waterproof, so in toilets and at wash counters we use compact laminate, which does not soak up water.

highlights.v: Yes, sand and prime first
No, the oil is the treatment
The first coat of lacquer acts as primer
Absorbs most and gets an extra coat
Stain-blocking primer under light paint
Compact laminate instead of plywood

h1: Calculating the sound absorption of perforated plywood
lead: The sound absorption we show for perforated plywood is calculated, not measured on our own board. Here is how the calculation is made and how it is calibrated against publicly available measurements, so an acoustician can check it.
body:
The sound absorption we show for acoustic walls in perforated plywood is based on a model we have calibrated against publicly available measurements of perforated panels from manufacturers' data sheets and a diploma thesis. This page explains how the sound absorption is calculated, which measurements it is calibrated against, and how well it performs.

These are the same figures shown on the page about [acoustic walls in perforated plywood](/akustikvaegge-perforeret-krydsfiner) and in the [acoustic designer](https://designer.neminventar.dk/designer?p=akustik) (in Danish).

## The panel and the holes

The panel is 12 mm plywood with round holes that go straight through without counterboring. The holes are calculated with Maa's model as short tubes: the air in each hole has a mass, and friction against the wall of the hole gives a resistance. Both depend on the hole diameter d, the panel thickness t, the open area ε and the frequency. At the ends of the hole a little extra air moves along, and it is calculated as an end correction of δ · d · F(ε), where F(ε) = 1 − 1.47 · √ε + 0.47 · ε^1.5 accounts for the neighbouring holes influencing each other. Maa uses δ = 0.85, and the calibration has set δ to 1.49. The panel is treated as rigid, so the wood species is not part of the calculation, only the thickness, the holes and the open area.

The open area is the part of the panel that is holes. In a square hole grid it is π · d² / (4 · c²), where c is the centre-to-centre distance. The Standard pattern has holes of 0.8 cm at 1.6 cm centres, which makes the grid 19.6 % open. The panels are 60 cm wide and 240 cm high with a 2 cm border without holes, and across the whole panel the open area is 18.1 %. That is the figure the calculation uses. In the Dense pattern the holes sit in staggered rows with a row spacing of c · √3 / 2, so the distance to all neighbours is the same.

## The cavity and the mineral wool

Behind the panel is a cavity against a rigid wall. The mineral wool is calculated with Miki's model from the airflow resistivity σ of the wool, and the rest of the cavity is air. The panel, the wool and the air are calculated as layers one after another, which gives the impedance of the surface.

We do not know the wool in the individual project, so σ is assumed: about 15 kPa·s/m² for mineral wool of about 30 kg/m³. If the acoustician's report or the wool's data sheet states a different wool, that is what applies.

When the wool lies against the back of the panel, the air from the holes is pushed out into the wool. This adds a resistance of σ · k · d / ε, where the calibration has set k to 0.51. All our figures are calculated with the wool against the panel, either in a 4.5 cm cavity filled with mineral wool or in a 9.5 cm cavity with 5 cm mineral wool against the panel and 4.5 cm air behind. 53 of the 54 measurements the model is calibrated against are also calculated with the wool against the panel, but for 30 of them the data sheet does not say where the wool lies.

The cavity is calculated as extended-reacting. Sound also travels obliquely through the air and the wool behind the panel, as in a cavity without partitions. The calibration chose this over a locally reacting cavity because it performed better on measurements the model had not seen: the mean error per octave band was 0.117 versus 0.126.

## From impedance to αp and αw

In a reverberation room, sound arrives from all directions. We calculate the absorption for 90 angles of incidence from 0 to 90 degrees and combine them using Paris' formula for a diffuse field. Under ISO 354 a sample of 10 to 12 m² is measured, and a sample of that size absorbs more sound than an infinite surface, especially below about 1000 Hz, because sound bends around the edges of the sample. We therefore calculate with a blend of the infinite surface and Thomasson's radiation impedance for a 3.0 by 3.6 m sample, and the calibration has set the sample's share to 0.49. That makes the figures comparable with measurements in reverberation rooms, and α can exceed 1 in a third-octave band, as in a measurement.

At 2000 to 4000 Hz the manufacturers' measurements lie 0.1 to 0.4 above the pure physics, more the larger the open area. We cover this with an addition that has no physical model behind it and is only calibrated: α' = 1 − (1 − α) · (1 − g), where g = 0.57 · min(1, ε / 0.28) · h(f). h(f) is 0 up to 500 Hz and 1 from 2000 Hz and rises linearly in log f in between.

The calculation gives α in third-octave bands from 100 to 5000 Hz. Under EN ISO 11654 the practical sound absorption coefficient αp in an octave band is the mean of the three third-octave bands, rounded to 0.05 and at most 1.00. The weighted sound absorption coefficient αw is found by shifting the reference curve, which is 0.80 at 250 Hz, 1.00 from 500 to 2000 Hz and 0.90 at 4000 Hz, downwards in steps of 0.05 until the sum of the unfavourable deviations is at most 0.10. αw is the value of the curve at 500 Hz. The absorption class follows from αw: A from 0.90, B from 0.80, C from 0.60, D from 0.30 and E from 0.15.

With the Standard pattern and 4.5 cm mineral wool, αp is 0.60, 0.95, 0.90, 0.70 and 0.55 from 250 to 4000 Hz. Shifted by 0.25, the curve lies 0.05 above αp at 2000 Hz and 0.10 above at 4000 Hz, 0.15 in total. Shifted by 0.30, the sum is 0.05, so αw is 0.70 and the absorption class C. At 500 Hz αp lies 0.25 above the shifted curve, so the shape indicator is M. With a 9.5 cm cavity and 5 cm mineral wool this also applies at 250 Hz, which gives αw 0.70 (LM). 125 Hz is not part of αw, which is why we always show αp per octave alongside.

## Calibration against 54 measurements

We have collected 62 publicly available measurements of perforated panels, 61 from five manufacturers' data sheets and one from a diploma thesis. Eight are left out because the holes were drilled larger from the back, or because the front had grooves with holes from behind. Those are not holes like ours. The 54 we use are 53 panels from the manufacturers and a fibre cement panel from the diploma thesis, all with through holes. The model assumes the figures were measured in a reverberation room under ISO 354, but we have not been able to verify this for every measurement. For one manufacturer the data sheet's graph calls the curve predicted. That is probably a typo for practical, but we do not know for certain that the curve was measured.

The measurements cover open areas from 1.9 to 39 %, holes from 0.5 to 1.2 cm, cavities from 2.5 to 35 cm and panels from 10 to 16 mm. 53 are calculated with mineral wool against the panel, and one has polyester felt against the wall with air in between. According to the data sheet, 31 have a fleece on the back of the panel and are calculated with it. 22 are figures from tables, and 32 are read off graphs or have a less clear method. The data sheets rarely state the full build-up, and where they do not, we have assumed it: the panel thickness for 29 of the measurements, where the wool lies for 30, the cavity depth for 13 and the hole pattern for 12. For 7 the data sheet does not say what lies behind the panel, and we have calculated with mineral wool as in another manufacturer's equivalent build-up. The 22 where the data sheet does not say whether there is a fleece are calculated without. The airflow resistivity σ is assumed from the type of wool and, where stated, its density. Only for the felt in the diploma thesis is it measured.

The calibration adjusts six quantities in the model so the error against the measurements is minimised, and the airflow resistivity σ is held fixed. Figures from tables weigh 1.0 and the others 0.6. The source with the most measurements weighs half, so it does not drive the calibration on its own, and measurements from the same source that the model calculates with exactly the same build-up share the weight.

| Quantity | What it does | Value |
|---|---|---|
| End correction δ | The air moving along at the ends of the holes | 1.49 (Maa: 0.85) |
| Wool against the panel, k | Extra resistance σ · k · d / ε | 0.51 |
| Sample size | Share of the difference between an infinite surface and a 10.8 m² sample | 0.49 |
| High-frequency addition | Largest addition at 2000 to 4000 Hz | 0.57 |
| Limit of the addition | The addition is full from this open area | 28 % |
| Fleece on the back | The fleece's resistance R, in the holes R / ε | 26 Pa·s/m |
| The cavity | Locally or extended-reacting | Extended |

The fleece is included because many of the measurements have one. Our own figures are calculated without fleece. Without calibration, the pure physics came out on average 0.22 too low for αw across the 54 measurements.

## How well the calculation performs

To see how well the model predicts measurements it has not seen, we calibrated it six times, each time without one source's measurements, and calculated the left-out ones with it. That way αw was on average 0.08 off, and four times out of five within 0.15. On average the calculation was 0.025 below the measurements. For the source the model predicted worst, αw was on average 0.15 below the measurements, and for another 0.12 above.

| Octave band | Mean error | Four out of five within |
|---|---|---|
| 125 Hz | 0.12 | 0.21 |
| 250 Hz | 0.19 | 0.30 |
| 500 Hz | 0.12 | 0.20 |
| 1000 Hz | 0.10 | 0.17 |
| 2000 Hz | 0.08 | 0.15 |
| 4000 Hz | 0.09 | 0.16 |
| αw | 0.08 | 0.15 |

The error is the difference between calculated and measured α, both capped at 1. The right-hand column is the uncertainty we work with: four out of five of the left-out measurements lay within it.

## Where the calculation performs worst

The bass is hardest, and the error is largest at 250 Hz. Below 5 % open area (13 measurements) the air in the holes becomes heavy, and the model's physics is weakest. Here the calculation was on average 0.20 off at 125 Hz and 0.22 at 250 Hz, against 0.12 and 0.19 for all measurements. The Sparse hole pattern has 4.7 % open area and falls in that range.

With 2 to 10 cm of air between the wool and the wall (8 measurements), the calculation was on average 0.18 off at 125 Hz and 0.13 at 2000 Hz, against 0.12 and 0.08 for all. The build-up with a 9.5 cm cavity and 5 cm mineral wool has 4.5 cm of air and belongs here. Where the wool fills the cavity with at most 2 cm of air, as in the 4.5 cm build-up (25 measurements), αw was on average 0.09 off.

Above 25 % open area (8 measurements), αw was on average 0.13 off and 500 Hz 0.23. Our four hole patterns have between 4.7 and 20.7 % open area. Below 1.9 % and above 39 % open area we are outside what the measurements cover, and the designer says so when a custom hole pattern goes that far. The model is not calibrated against any measurement with an empty cavity, so we do not calculate it.

## Reverberation time in the room

In the designer's Room step we calculate the reverberation time with Sabine's formula, T = 0.161 · V / A, for each octave band from 125 to 4000 Hz. V is the room volume in m³, and A is the room's absorption in m², the sum of each surface's area times its α. The acoustic wall replaces a section of wall, so with panels A = A without + S · (αp − α of the wall), where S is the panel area.

The room's surfaces are calculated with typical table values from a public materials database compiled from measurements under ISO 354. The furniture is treated as part of the floor with a share we have assumed: wooden tables and chairs on a quarter of the floor in a classroom and a fifth in a daycare centre, and desks with upholstered chairs on a sixth in an office. The room is calculated furnished and unoccupied, as the requirement applies. The ceiling is the choice that moves the most.

| Surface | 125 Hz | 250 Hz | 500 Hz | 1000 Hz | 2000 Hz | 4000 Hz |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Light plasterboard walls with windows and doors | 0.15 | 0.10 | 0.06 | 0.04 | 0.04 | 0.05 |
| Linoleum on concrete | 0.02 | 0.03 | 0.03 | 0.03 | 0.03 | 0.02 |
| Wooden tables and chairs | 0.05 | 0.08 | 0.10 | 0.12 | 0.12 | 0.12 |
| Hard ceiling of concrete or plaster | 0.01 | 0.01 | 0.02 | 0.02 | 0.02 | 0.05 |
| Perforated plasterboard ceiling | 0.45 | 0.55 | 0.60 | 0.90 | 0.86 | 0.75 |
| Mineral wool acoustic ceiling | 0.48 | 0.97 | 1.00 | 0.97 | 1.00 | 1.00 |
| Acoustic wall, Standard, 4.5 cm mineral wool | 0.25 | 0.60 | 0.95 | 0.90 | 0.70 | 0.55 |

One example is a classroom of 9 by 7 metres with 3 metres to the ceiling, 189 m³, with a perforated plasterboard ceiling. At 250 Hz, A = 96 · 0.10 + 63 · 0.03 + 63 · 0.55 + 15.75 · 0.08 = 47.4 m² for walls, floor, ceiling and furniture, and T = 0.161 · 189 / 47.4 = 0.64 s. With 7.2 m² of panels, A = 47.4 + 7.2 · (0.60 − 0.10) = 51.0 m², and T = 0.60 s. The panel area needed in each octave band is S = (0.161 · V / requirement − A without) / (αp − α of the wall), and the largest of them applies. Here it is 6.6 m² at 250 Hz. With a hard ceiling about 250 m² would be needed at 125 Hz, which is more than the room's four walls of 96 m².

We calculate without the air's own absorption and with Sabine rather than Eyring. Both give a slightly too long reverberation time in rooms with a lot of absorption, so the calculation errs on the safe side and gives more panels, never fewer.

The requirements are in the guidance on acoustic conditions to the Danish Building Regulations, BR18. In classrooms the maximum is 0.6 seconds and in common rooms for group work 0.4 seconds (educational buildings, table 3.4), and in playrooms in daycare centres 0.4 seconds (table 4.4), in every octave band from 125 to 4000 Hz. At 125 Hz the value may be 20 % higher, and the requirements apply in furnished rooms. Sports halls must have at most 1.6 seconds below 3500 m³ and 1.8 seconds above, calculated unfurnished. For offices and meeting rooms, 0.6 seconds is a suggested design value in the guidance for office buildings, not a requirement. Outside Denmark, the national requirements apply, and the acoustician sets the values.

## What the figures are not

The figures are a calculation. They are not a test report, and they are not a guarantee of the sound absorption or the reverberation time in a project. None of the measurements are of our own panel, and only a measurement of it can show how well the figures match that panel. The actual reverberation time depends on the room's actual surfaces, windows, doors and furniture, on the cavity and the wool behind the panels and on where the panels are placed.

Use the figures to choose a hole pattern and build-up, and to see whether wall panels alone can meet the requirement. The acoustician calculates the real room and sets the project's values, and the reverberation time is measured in the finished room. [Send us the acoustician's report](/kontakt?emne=Akustikv%C3%A6g) together with the drawings, and we will match the hole pattern and build-up to it.

faq.q: Are the figures measured on your panel?
faq.a: No. The figures are calculated. The model is calibrated against 54 publicly available measurements of perforated panels from manufacturers' data sheets and a diploma thesis, and none of them are of our own panel. The figures are an estimate for choosing a hole pattern and build-up, and the acoustician's calculation decides the project.

faq.q: How accurate is the calculation?
faq.a: On measurements the model had not seen, αw was on average 0.08 off, and four times out of five within 0.15. Per octave band the uncertainty is largest at 250 Hz, where four out of five lay within 0.30, and smallest at 2000 Hz, within 0.15. Below 5 % open area the bass is most uncertain.

faq.q: Which models is the calculation based on?
faq.a: The holes in the panel are calculated with Maa's model and a calibrated end correction, and the mineral wool with Miki's model from the airflow resistivity. The cavity is calculated as extended-reacting and the diffuse field as a calibrated blend of an infinite surface and a 10.8 m² sample, as in a reverberation room. αp, αw and the absorption class are calculated under EN ISO 11654.

faq.q: Which mineral wool do you assume?
faq.a: Mineral wool of about 30 kg/m³ with an airflow resistivity of about 15 kPa·s/m², placed against the back of the panel, either in a 4.5 cm cavity filled with wool or in a 9.5 cm cavity with 5 cm of wool. The value is assumed. If the acoustician's report or the data sheet states a different wool, that is what applies.

faq.q: Why is 125 Hz not part of αw?
faq.a: That is how αw is defined in EN ISO 11654: it is calculated from 250 to 4000 Hz. The reverberation time requirement in the Danish Building Regulations applies from 125 Hz, so two build-ups with the same αw can meet the requirement differently. That is why we always show αp per octave alongside αw.

faq.q: Can the calculation be used as documentation?
faq.a: Not on its own. It shows what we have assumed and can be used to choose a build-up, but it is not a test report. The basis is the acoustician's calculation of the room, and the reverberation time is measured in the finished room.

54 publicly available measurements
Maa for the holes, Miki for the mineral wool
αw on average 0.08 off
αp and αw under EN ISO 11654
Sabine's formula against the BR18 requirements

h1: How much does a made to measure fitted wardrobe cost?
lead: A made to measure wardrobe in oak veneer, 60 cm wide, 210 cm high and 60 cm deep, costs DKK 9,188 including Danish VAT, delivered flat-packed to the kerb. Here is the calculation behind the price, and what it comes to for a whole wall. All prices apply to delivery in Denmark.
body:
If the wardrobe is to arrive assembled, be carried in and installed by us, the same wardrobe costs DKK 13,838. The wardrobe is the same, and the difference is how it gets into the room. The wardrobes are delivered flat-packed with assembly instructions, and that is how all the wardrobe prices on this page are calculated. In the [designer](https://designer.neminventar.dk/designer?p=hoejskab) (in Danish) you see the price of your own wardrobe while you build it.

## The full price in four examples

The table adds up the parts for four orders in oak veneer. The wardrobes come first in the calculation, and what comes on top is explained further down, so you can check the sums. All figures are in Danish kroner including Danish VAT and were calculated in the designer on 20 October 2026.

| Example in oak veneer | The calculation | Total |
|---|---|---|
| One wardrobe, flat-packed and delivered to the kerb | DKK 8,500 + 688 | [DKK 9,188](https://designer.neminventar.dk/designer?p=hoejskab&t=e30) |
| One wardrobe, assembled, carried in and installed | DKK 8,500 + 525 + 4,813 | [DKK 13,838](https://designer.neminventar.dk/designer?p=hoejskab&t=e30) |
| Three wardrobes side by side, flat-packed and carried in, with measuring | DKK 25,500 + 2,063 + 3,125 | [DKK 30,688](https://designer.neminventar.dk/designer?p=hoejskab&t=eyJuIjozfQ) |
| Two wardrobes and a bench with a top cabinet, flat-packed and carried in | DKK 25,300 + 2,063 | [DKK 27,363](https://designer.neminventar.dk/designer?p=hoejskab&t=eyJuIjozLCJtIjpbeyJpIjoxLCJ0IjoiYmFlbmsifV19) |

All wardrobes and the bench are 60 cm wide, so both walls are 180 cm wide. The bench stands between the two wardrobes with two drawers, a cushion in grey upholstery fabric and a top cabinet above. Read more about [the bench](/opbevaringsbaenk) and [top cabinets](/overskabe) (in Danish).

## The material moves the price most

The same wardrobe can cost more than four times as much just because the material is different. The table shows the wardrobe from the examples, 60 cm wide, 210 cm high and 60 cm deep, without delivery.

| Material | One wardrobe |
|---|---|
| White melamine | [DKK 4,450](https://designer.neminventar.dk/designer?p=hoejskab&t=eyJtYXQiOiJtZWxhbWluIn0) |
| Beech, oak or ash veneer | DKK 8,450-9,200 |
| Pine or birch plywood | DKK 9,950-12,000 |
| Compact laminate or pre-finished veneer | DKK 18,575-19,375 |

It is the board that costs. White melamine is a chipboard with a white surface and is the cheapest. Veneer is a thin layer of real wood on MDF and the cheapest wood, and plywood is wood all the way through, so the layers show on the edge. In the most expensive row, the board is either laminate all the way through, which takes water and wear, or veneer from selected logs with an even, calm grain, where the surface is already finished when we receive the board. What the materials look like on a wardrobe is shown under [made to measure wardrobes](/garderobeskab) and [plywood cabinets](/skabe-i-krydsfiner).

## Dimensions and options

One dimension has a jump in price, and that is the depth. The sides of the wardrobe are cut from boards that are about 122 to 125 cm wide. At 60 cm depth two sides can be cut from the width of the board, at 62 cm only one. That is why a wardrobe in oak veneer costs [DKK 8,575](https://designer.neminventar.dk/designer?p=hoejskab&t=eyJkIjo2MX0) at 61 cm and [DKK 11,125](https://designer.neminventar.dk/designer?p=hoejskab&t=eyJkIjo2Mn0) at 62 cm. With a hanging rail the wardrobe must be at least 60 cm deep.

The table shows what the other dimensions and the options add or subtract on one wardrobe in oak veneer. On a wardrobe wall you choose the interior wardrobe by wardrobe, so an addition applies to each wardrobe that has it.

| One wardrobe in oak veneer | Difference |
|---|---|
| Top cabinet above, 30 to 50 cm | +DKK 1,975 to +2,875 |
| 80 cm wide with two doors | +DKK 2,200 |
| Doors in coloured oil | +DKK 2,000 |
| Two drawers at the bottom | +DKK 1,950 |
| Four shelves instead of a hanging rail | +DKK 875 |
| 240 cm high instead of 210 cm | +DKK 825 |
| Inset door or 170° hinges | +DKK 325 each |
| 40 cm deep, with shelves | -DKK 775 |

The drawers in the table are ordinary drawers on runners. Drawers in solid wood with finger joints can also be chosen, and their price is stated in the offer.

## Flat-packed or assembled

The wardrobes come flat-packed with assembly instructions, and you assemble them yourself in the room where they will stand. If you want them assembled from the workshop, there is a freight surcharge, DKK 525 for a wardrobe 60 cm wide, 210 cm high and 60 cm deep. The surcharge only covers freight and follows the size and number of wardrobes.

Installation, where we carry the wardrobes in and put them up, is only available with assembled wardrobes. Flat-packed, the wardrobes can be delivered to the kerb or carried in.

## Delivery, installation and measuring

Delivery is calculated for the whole order and is priced in the designer's basket before you send.

| Delivery for the whole order | One wardrobe | Three wardrobes |
|---|---|---|
| Flat-packed to the kerb | DKK 688 | DKK 1,188 |
| Flat-packed and carried in | DKK 1,313 | DKK 2,063 |
| Assembled, carried in and installed | DKK 4,813 | DKK 8,563 |

Three wardrobes do not cost three times as much to deliver as one, so on a long wall delivery takes up less of the price. With installation, the surcharge for assembled wardrobes comes on top, as in the second example above. Measuring can be added for the whole order and costs DKK 3,125.

## From price to offer

When you send the wardrobes from the designer, it is an enquiry, not an order. We send an offer and a drawing with the final dimensions, and you approve the drawing before the wardrobes are made in our own production. It takes 3 to 6 weeks from order to delivery, and we deliver across Denmark.

The designer shows the wardrobes freestanding, but we draw them to fit the room. If they are to stand in a niche or go up to the ceiling, say so in the message. If the designer cannot do what you want, [send us a sketch](/kontakt?emne=Garderobeskab). You can read about wardrobes for high ceilings and niches under [made to measure wardrobes in Copenhagen](/garderobeskabe-efter-maal-koebenhavn) (in Danish).

faq.q: How much does a made to measure wardrobe cost?
faq.a: A wardrobe 60 cm wide, 210 cm high and 60 cm deep, with a hat shelf and hanging rail, costs from DKK 4,450 including Danish VAT in white melamine and up to DKK 19,375 in pre-finished veneer, flat-packed and without delivery. In oak veneer and delivered to the kerb it costs DKK 9,188. The prices apply to delivery in Denmark.

faq.q: Is delivery included in the price?
faq.a: No. Delivery is calculated for the whole order and is priced in the designer's basket before you send. Flat-packed to the kerb it costs DKK 688 for one wardrobe and DKK 1,188 for three wardrobes.

faq.q: How much does it cost to have the wardrobe assembled and installed?
faq.a: An assembled wardrobe carries a freight surcharge, DKK 525 for a wardrobe 60 cm wide. Delivery where we carry the wardrobe in and install it costs DKK 4,813 for one wardrobe and DKK 8,563 for three. Installation is only available with assembled wardrobes.

faq.q: How much does measuring cost?
faq.a: Measuring can be added and costs DKK 3,125 for the whole order.

faq.q: Why is a wardrobe 62 cm deep so much more expensive?
faq.a: The sides of the wardrobe are cut from boards about 122 to 125 cm wide. At 60 cm depth two sides can be cut from the width of the board, at 62 cm only one. A wardrobe in oak veneer costs DKK 8,575 at 61 cm and DKK 11,125 at 62 cm.

faq.q: How much does a wardrobe wall with a bench cost?
faq.a: Two wardrobes with a bench in between, all 60 cm wide, where the bench has two drawers, a cushion and a top cabinet, cost DKK 25,300 in oak veneer, flat-packed and without delivery. A [bench](/opbevaringsbaenk) on its own, 100 cm wide and 40 cm deep, with two drawers and a cushion costs DKK 6,375 in oak veneer.

faq.q: Is the price in the designer the final price?
faq.a: The price in the designer applies to the wardrobes as you have built them. When you send them, it is an enquiry, and we send an offer and a drawing with the final dimensions, which you approve before the wardrobes are made. The price of drawers in solid wood with finger joints is stated in the offer.

highlights.v: DKK 9,188 incl. Danish VAT in oak veneer
DKK 13,838 for the same wardrobe
Can more than quadruple the price
For the whole order, priced in the basket
DKK 3,125 for the whole order
3-6 weeks, across Denmark
